query: Earlier studies of conventional metallic multilayers provide a general framework for deformation, but its conclusions may not transfer directly to high-entropy-alloy systems because compositional complexity, severe lattice distortion, and short-range order are associated with unusual deformation behavior. Preliminary evidence from FCC/BCC high-entropy-alloy multilayers remains insufficient to establish what controls creep or when a given response dominates. Within the constraints of retaining a nanoscale multilayer coating and balancing strength with deformation tolerance, what testable mechanistic hypothesis could explain progressive plastic deformation under sustained loading? State what governs the behavior and why, an unspecified controlled comparison that would expose it, predicted observations relative to the starting baseline, boundary conditions, relevant prior support, and a result that would falsify the hypothesis.

generation.hypothesis: Progressive plastic deformation (creep) in high-entropy alloy multilayers under sustained loading is primarily governed by interface‐mediated dislocation climb that is modulated by a moderate negative lattice misfit and maintained short-range order between the FCC and BCC layers; this behavior is attributed to the severe lattice distortion that provides pronounced solid-solution strengthening.
generation.material_initial_state: A nanoscale multilayer coating consisting of alternating FCC and BCC high-entropy alloy layers that inherently exhibit severe lattice distortion and local short-range order.
generation.intervention: Application of a sustained load under creep conditions at an elevated temperature while systematically tuning the lattice misfit via compositional adjustments between the multilayer interfaces.
generation.conditions: Elevated temperature and constant applied stress within the regime where the nanoscale multilayer structure remains intact. Comparisons are made between multilayers with a moderate negative lattice misfit and those with either near-zero or excessively negative misfit.
generation.structural_mediator: The interfaces between the FCC and BCC layers, where a moderate negative lattice misfit—together with local short-range order arising from compositional complexity—stabilizes the phase boundary and controls the activation of dislocation climb.
generation.mechanism: Severe lattice distortion (a hallmark of solid-solution strengthening) and local short-range order create a heterogeneous energy landscape that limits long-range dislocation glide. Under sustained loading, dislocation climb becomes the dominant creep mechanism at these interfaces. A moderate negative lattice misfit enhances interfacial stability by promoting robust chemical short-range order and significant solid-solution strengthening, thereby retarding rapid creep, whereas non-optimized misfit leads to higher localized strain and accelerated deformation.
generation.predicted_outcome: Multilayers engineered to have a moderate negative lattice misfit will display reduced creep rates, more uniform plastic deformation, and lower atomic strain at the interfaces compared to multilayers with near-zero or excessively negative misfit.
generation.baseline: Multilayers with non-optimized lattice misfit (either near-zero or overly negative) that show accelerated creep deformation, higher localized strain, and more pronounced nonuniform plasticity.
generation.boundary: This hypothesis is expected to be valid as long as the nanoscale multilayer architecture is retained and operating conditions favor dislocation climb over other mechanisms (e.g., when temperatures and stresses do not induce layer delamination or complete phase transitions). It may not apply in regimes where secondary phenomena (such as delamination) dominate.
generation.uncertainty: The relative quantitative contributions of chemical short-range order versus lattice misfit in governing the creep rate remain to be precisely determined. Additionally, the interplay of these factors may vary with specific alloy compositions and processing histories.

falsification_experiment.design: Fabricate two groups of HEA multilayer coatings that are identical in layer thickness and overall composition, differing only in the achieved lattice misfit at the interfaces: one group with a moderate negative misfit (optimized) and one with either near-zero or excessive misfit (non-optimized). Subject each group to identical sustained loading (creep) tests at elevated but controlled temperatures while monitoring the deformation process in situ using techniques such as high-resolution TEM or nanoindentation-based creep measurement.
measurements: Dislocation density and evolution at the interfaces
Atomic strain distribution and interface integrity
Onset of localized deformation or premature failure
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the multilayers with moderate negative lattice misfit do not exhibit a significantly lower creep rate and more uniform plastic deformation compared to the non-optimized samples, or if the anticipated relationship between lattice misfit magnitude and creep performance is not observed (i.e., if non-optimized samples perform as well or better), the hypothesis would be falsified.

cited_evidence.text: As shown in Figure 13, all creep curves exhibit the typical three-stage behavior. Notably, the duration of the steady-state creep stage decreases with increasing |δ|. The relationship between creep life and |δ| is non-monotonic. Specifically, within the range of −0.1688% to −0.084%, creep life increases as |δ| increases. Conversely, within the range of −0.8075% to −0.1688%, creep life decreases as |δ| increases. The longest creep life is observed at δ = −0.1688%. To gain further insight into the underlying mechanisms, atomic strain distributions were analyzed, as shown in Figure 14. Figure 14a,b compare atomic strain maps of HESAs with negative (−0.1402%) and positive (0.1402%) lattice misfits. At t = 130 ps, the model with the negative lattice misfit (Figure 14a) exhibits lower atomic strain, suggesting enhanced resistance to deformation. This implies that a negative lattice misfit stabilizes the γ′ phase, strengthens the γ/γ′ interface, and impedes dislocation motion, thereby improving creep resistance. Notably, 5B approaches near-isotropic plasticity (AH = 1.012), corresponding to a substantial anisotropy reduction of 86.6%. This abrupt and disproportionate suppression of plastic anisotropy, with R jumping from 6.0% to 86.6%, indicates a distortion-mediated threshold effect in slip activation as δl increases from 1.29% to 1.31%, rather than a gradual homogenization of bonding stiffness. As indicated by Gianola et al., such high distortion levels in refractory multiprincipal element alloys equalized slip resistance across slip planes, facilitating the activation of rarely observed higher-order slip systems and promoting more uniform plastic deformation. At elevated temperatures, 1B softens significantly, consistent with the behavior of pure tungsten, , whereas 3B and 5B retain high hardness due to strong solid-solution strengthening and enhanced lattice friction from distortion. Specifically, severe lattice distortion substantially increases the Peierls barrier, restricting long-range dislocation glide and suppressing localized deformation under elevated temperatures, ,,, as reflected by the still significant anisotropy reduction ratio of 105.5% in 5B at HT.
